newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Italian, Albanian leaders meet on rebel territory.
newsitem.headline: Italian, Albanian leaders meet on rebel territory.

text.p: Italian and Albanian leaders, in a move to soothe strained ties, held tightly-guarded talks in a rebel-held Albanian town on Wednesday and reaffirmed plans for an Italian-led force to protect aid to the Balkan state.

"There is no political crisis between Italy and Albania," Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino said after the surprise meeting with Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi in the southern town of Gjirokaster.

Prodi, braving anti-Italian feeling after the sinking of an Albanian refugee ship off Italy last week in a collision with an Italian corvette, told parliament on his return to Rome that the meeting had removed "tensions and shadows".

The first foreign leader to visit Albania since an insurrection last month, Prodi flew in with three navy helicopters and about 25 Italian marines. He was also guarded by Fino's bodyguards, local police and forces of the local 'salvation committee'.

Tirana says at least 80 people died in Friday's sinking and many of the 34 survivors accused the Italians of ramming, charges the navy denies. Italy has sought to halt a flow of 13,000 refugees from the former communist state in March.
Prodi and Fino, formerly Socialist mayor of Gjirokaster, said deployment of the planned U.N.-approved force of some 5,000 men should go ahead unaffected by the sinking.

Prodi said 34-year-old Fino reconfirmed "the Albanian government's request for multinational forces". The force will help protect food and medical supplies to Europe's poorest country in the run-up to planned elections in June.
He later told parliament that Italy would try to recover the bodies of Albanians drowned in the tragedy and give "some form of assistance for families affected by the disaster."
Many Albanians along the road waved as Prodi passed in a convoy of cars from the small local airport, and there were no signs of hostility.

Heavily-armed rebel committees controlling southern towns, including Gjirokaster, want right-wing President Sali Berisha to resign. The committees say they are trying to stop the banditry and looting that has killed scores of people.

Berisha was forced to appoint 34-year-old Socialist Fino to head a unity government on March 11. Rebels blame Berisha for the collapse of popular savings schemes this year at the root of Albania's unrest.
Scores of people have died in Albania over the past month.
The state news agency ATA reported that an Italian firm making stationery and ornaments was set ablaze on Monday in Fushe-Kruje just north of the capital.

Rumours swept Tirana that the U.S. embassy might open its gates to would-be refugees, drawing scores of hopeful Albanians to the area. Armed police mounted heavy guard around the embassy compound and dispersed the crowds that gathered in nearby coffee shops.

Also on Wednesday, Fino's Socialist party agreed to take up their nine seats in parliament boycotted since elections last year, saying they wanted to help a return to political normality. Berisha's Democratic Party controls 122 of 140 seats.
After meeting Prodi, Fino left by helicopter to Greece for talks with Prime Minister Costas Simitis on the Italian-led force.
Fino and Simitis will also hold talks in Athens on Thursday with Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country holds the European Union presidency, and European mediator Frantz Vranitzky.

In Rome on Wednesday, Vranitzky said the planned multinational force was vital for Albania but that it had to avoid the sort of mistakes made in former Yugoslavia. He estimated the force could be ready in 10 to 14 days.
Fino also said Prodi had agreed to an invitation to visit Vlore, the rebel-held port from where the Albanian refugee vessel left and where anti-Italian passions are most fierce.
Vlore is also one of two ports that the multinational force is meant to secure. Military experts were meeting in Rome to work out details of the mission.

Italy will lead the force, aimed at securing the ports of Durres and Vlore and Tirana airport. So far Italy is expected to provide 2,000 to 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Spain 500 and Romania 400.
